title: How LLMs Generate: Tokens & the Context Window
summary: LLMs read and write text as tokens — sub-word chunks — and can only 'see' a fixed number of them at once: the context window. Every prompt, tool schema, past turn, and the answer itself competes for that one budget, which is why agents live or die by context management.

subtopics.title: Tokens, not words
subtopics.explanation: Models process text as tokens — common words are one token, rare words split into several, and whitespace/punctuation count too. A rough rule of thumb is ~4 characters per token in English. Everything about limits and cost is measured in tokens, so it pays to think in them, not words.

subtopics.title: The context window is a hard ceiling
subtopics.explanation: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one call (e.g. 8K, 128K, 200K depending on the model). Go over it and the request errors or silently drops content. It's the single most important number when designing an agent's memory.
subtopics.example:
WINDOW = 128_000  # model-specific
used = est_tokens(system) + est_tokens(tools) + est_tokens(history)
assert used < WINDOW, "trim history or summarise before calling"

subtopics.title: Everything shares one budget
subtopics.explanation: The window is split across the system prompt, tool schemas, the running conversation/history, retrieved documents, and the space left for the model's answer. Grow one and you shrink another. Agents feel this constantly because tool schemas and history pile up every turn.
subtopics.example:
budget = WINDOW
budget -= est_tokens(system_prompt)
budget -= est_tokens(tool_schemas)
budget -= RESERVED_FOR_ANSWER      # e.g. 2000
# whatever's left is what history + retrieved docs must fit in

subtopics.title: Overflow → truncation or eviction
subtopics.explanation: When history outgrows the budget, you must drop or compress something — usually the oldest turns — or the call fails. Naive truncation loses information the agent may need; that's exactly why summarization and memory (a later track) exist. Knowing where the cliff is lets you design before you fall off it.

subtopics.title: Tokens are how you pay (and wait)
subtopics.explanation: Providers bill per input and output token, and latency scales with tokens generated. A chatty agent that re-sends huge histories every loop is slow and expensive. Counting tokens is the foundation of both cost control and the streaming/latency work in the Production track.
subtopics.example:
cost = (in_tokens / 1000) * PRICE_IN + (out_tokens / 1000) * PRICE_OUT
# an agent that loops 8x re-sends the whole history each time -> multiply!

foundations.overview: Large language models don't read characters or words — they read tokens, sub-word units produced by a tokenizer. A model can only consider a fixed number of tokens at once, called the context window, and that window is a shared budget: the system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history, any retrieved documents, and the room reserved for the answer all draw from it. For agents this is the central constraint, because tool schemas and history accumulate every single loop, steadily eating the budget.
foundations.formalDefinition: A token is the atomic unit an LLM reads/writes (typically a sub-word piece). The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in a single forward pass; all inputs plus the generated output must fit within it.
foundations.whyItMatters: Every agent limitation — how much history it can keep, how many documents it can ground on, how much it costs, how long it takes — is ultimately a token-budget problem. You can't design agent memory, RAG, or cost controls without thinking in tokens.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a whiteboard of fixed size. The system prompt, tools, and every past turn are written on it; when it fills up you must erase something to write more. The context window is that whiteboard, measured in tokens.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Choosing a model by window size, trimming/summarizing history in long chats, budgeting how many retrieved chunks to include in RAG, and estimating the cost of an agent run before shipping it.
foundations.performanceImpact: Latency and price both scale with tokens; an agent that resends a large history on every loop can be an order of magnitude slower and costlier than one that compacts context.
commonUseCases: Choosing a model by context-window size

commonMisconceptions.reality: Common words are ~1 token, but rare words, code, and punctuation split into several. English averages ~4 characters per token — always estimate, don't assume.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A bigger context window means I never have to manage context.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Bigger windows cost more, get slower, and can dilute attention ('lost in the middle'). Good agents still curate context rather than dumping everything in.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The window only limits my input.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Input and the generated output share the same budget — if you fill the window with prompt, there's no room left for the answer.

interactiveWidget.title: Feel the context budget fill up
interactiveWidget.caption: The system prompt, tool schemas, and history already claim part of the window. Type or paste text and watch your tokens compete for the same budget — push it over and see what an agent must evict.

checkpoints.prompt: Using the ~4-chars-per-token rule, roughly how many tokens is the string "agentic AI"? (10 characters)
checkpoints.explanation: ≈ 10 characters / 4 ≈ 2–3 tokens. It's an estimate — real tokenizers differ — but the point is tokens ≪ characters and ≠ words.

checkpoints.prompt: An agent's chat keeps growing and eventually the API call fails. What's the root cause?
options: Total tokens (system + tools + history + answer) exceeded the context window
checkpoints.explanation: History accumulates each loop and shares the window with everything else. Once the total exceeds the window, the call fails — which is why you trim or summarize.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is resending a huge history on every agent loop a problem?
options: It improves accuracy so it's fine
Input tokens are re-billed and latency grows each loop
checkpoints.explanation: You pay for input tokens every call and latency scales with tokens, so a large history multiplied across many loops is both slow and expensive — motivating compaction and caching.

keyTakeaways: LLMs read/write tokens (sub-word units), roughly ~4 characters each — think in tokens, not words.
The context window is a hard ceiling on tokens per call; input and output share it.
System prompt, tool schemas, history, retrieved docs, and the answer all draw from one budget.
Overflow forces lossy truncation/eviction — the reason summarization and memory exist.
Tokens drive both cost and latency, so counting them underpins every optimization.
